```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
here::i_am("posts/inflation-unemployment/index.qmd")
POST_DIR <- here::here("posts", "inflation-unemployment")
a <- readRDS(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/analysis.rds"))
f <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
date_label <- function(x) format(x, "%B %Y")
qval <- function(label, variable) a$quarterly[[variable]][a$quarterly$label == label]
point <- function(date, variable) a$monthly[[variable]][a$monthly$date == as.Date(date)]
provenance <- read.csv(file.path(POST_DIR, "data/raw/provenance.csv"))
```

## One adjustment, two stages

U.S. inflation fell sharply after its 2022 peak, while unemployment increased much less. That comparison raises a specific question. How much did unemployment rise, and did it rise throughout the period when inflation was falling? The distinction matters because an endpoint comparison can hide when workers faced a weakening labor market.

I use monthly data from 2015 through 2024 to put the adjustment in context. The earlier years provide a benchmark for comparing similar unemployment rates under different inflation conditions. The main finding is that the adjustment occurred in two stages. Inflation initially declined substantially with little change in unemployment. Later, unemployment rose while inflation declined more slowly. These are descriptions of the observed path, not estimates of what a policy required or caused.

## Measuring the two rates

The data come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics through FRED. The series are [CPIAUCSL](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL), the all-items consumer price index, and [UNRATE](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/UNRATE), the unemployment rate. Both series are seasonally adjusted. Unemployment measures unemployed people as a share of the civilian labor force, not the entire population.

I calculate inflation as `100 × (CPI this month / CPI twelve months earlier − 1)`. An extra year of CPI data supplies the initial comparison, leaving `r nrow(a$monthly)` matched monthly observations. This is a growth rate, rather than the CPI's index level. Falling positive inflation means prices are increasing more slowly, not necessarily falling. Because the calculation uses seasonally adjusted CPI, it can differ slightly from the commonly reported year-over-year rate based on unadjusted CPI.

## When did inflation and unemployment turn?

Before comparing the two rates directly, Figure 1 establishes their timing. The aligned panels let us see whether their peaks and declines occurred together.

```{r}
#| label: fig-timeline
#| fig-cap: "Aligned monthly series with a common vertical scale. The unemployment spike precedes the inflation peak."
#| fig-alt: "Two time-series panels show unemployment surging in 2020 and inflation peaking in 2022."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/timeline.png"))
```

Figure 1 shows unemployment reaching `r f(a$u_peak$UNRATE)`% in `r date_label(a$u_peak$date)`, when inflation was only `r f(a$u_peak$inflation)`%. Inflation instead peaked at `r f(a$peak$inflation)`% in `r date_label(a$peak$date)`, with unemployment at `r f(a$peak$UNRATE)`%. The unemployment peak preceded the inflation peak, so treating the entire episode as one simultaneous movement would miss its sequence.

By `r date_label(a$end$date)`, inflation was `r f(a$end$inflation)`% and unemployment was `r f(a$end$UNRATE)`%. Relative to the inflation peak, inflation declined `r f(a$peak$inflation - a$end$inflation)` percentage points while unemployment rose `r f(a$end$UNRATE - a$peak$UNRATE)` points. That endpoint comparison measures the overall movement. To understand it, we first need to ask whether the same unemployment rate has consistently been associated with similar inflation.

## Did similar unemployment mean similar inflation?

Figure 2 pairs the two rates month by month. Colors and shapes distinguish calendar periods so that an apparent relationship across all observations does not obscure differences between episodes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Each point pairs inflation and unemployment in the same month. Period boundaries are descriptive calendar groupings, not estimated structural breaks."
#| fig-alt: "A scatterplot distinguishes pre-COVID months, 2020-2021, and 2022-2024 using both colors and shapes."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/scatter.png"))
```

The points occupy different parts of the chart across periods. Before COVID, relatively low unemployment coexisted with modest inflation. During 2020 and 2021, high-unemployment months had low inflation, while inflation rose as unemployment receded. From 2022 through 2024, inflation varied widely within a much narrower unemployment range.

For a concrete comparison, unemployment was `r f(point("2019-12-01", "UNRATE"))`% in December 2019 and `r f(point("2022-06-01", "UNRATE"))`% in June 2022, but inflation was `r f(point("2019-12-01", "inflation"))`% and `r f(point("2022-06-01", "inflation"))`%, respectively. Similar unemployment therefore did not imply similar inflation. But this scatterplot loses the order of the observations. Did the later decline in inflation come before, during, or after unemployment began to rise?

## How did the adjustment unfold after 2022?

Figure 3 reconnects observations in time order. I average each rate over three months to make the path easier to follow, at the cost of hiding monthly fluctuations. Downward movement means falling inflation, and rightward movement means rising unemployment. Arrows point toward the next quarter. The narrower horizontal scale makes small unemployment changes visible; distances should not be compared with Figure 2.

```{r}
#| label: fig-path
#| fig-cap: "Arrows connect consecutive quarters from 2022 through 2024. Both coordinates are averages of monthly rates; the horizontal scale is deliberately narrower than in Figure 2."
#| fig-alt: "A chronological quarterly path shows inflation falling sharply in 2023 with little unemployment movement, followed by a rise in unemployment during 2024."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/path.png"))
```

Figure 3 restores the time ordering lost in the scatterplot. Between 2022 Q2 and 2023 Q2, average inflation fell from `r f(qval("2022 Q2", "inflation"))`% to `r f(qval("2023 Q2", "inflation"))`%, while unemployment moved from `r f(qval("2022 Q2", "unemployment"))`% to `r f(qval("2023 Q2", "unemployment"))`%. Much of that initial disinflation occurred without rising unemployment. By 2024 Q4, unemployment had increased to `r f(qval("2024 Q4", "unemployment"))`%, with inflation at `r f(qval("2024 Q4", "inflation"))`%. From 2023 Q2 to 2024 Q4, unemployment rose `r f(qval("2024 Q4", "unemployment") - qval("2023 Q2", "unemployment"))` percentage points, while inflation fell a further `r f(qval("2023 Q2", "inflation") - qval("2024 Q4", "inflation"))` points. That later stage combined a clearer increase in unemployment with a slower decline in inflation.

## What the two stages tell us

The answer depends on the interval. From the monthly inflation peak to December 2024, unemployment rose `r f(a$end$UNRATE - a$peak$UNRATE)` percentage points as inflation fell `r f(a$peak$inflation - a$end$inflation)` points. The quarterly path reveals what that summary hides. Much of the initial inflation decline occurred with unemployment nearly unchanged, followed by a period of rising unemployment and smaller additional inflation declines.

This pattern does not establish that reducing inflation is always costless, or that a particular policy caused either movement. Supply conditions, demand, expectations, and policy may all matter, and these two series cannot separate their contributions. The calendar groups are descriptive, not estimated structural breaks. National averages also conceal differences between workers and households.

The central takeaway is specific to this episode. Falling inflation and rising unemployment did not move together at a constant pace. Looking at the sequence reveals both the early improvement and the later labor market weakening that an endpoint comparison alone misses.

---

**Data and replication:** BLS series distributed by FRED, downloaded `r substr(provenance$retrieved_utc[1], 1, 10)`. These are revised historical observations, not real-time vintages. [Code, saved data, and instructions](https://github.com/yipin-grena/aeds6400-blog/tree/main/posts/inflation-unemployment) reproduce all figures and reported numbers.
